idiom_name: class per page with By locators and descriptor-based element wrappers (selenium-python tutorial)
implementation_notes: The selenium-python guide is the canonical Python realization: a base page class stores the driver, each page class holds locator classes/constants and action methods (click_go_button, is_results_found), and element access can be wrapped in a descriptor class whose __get__/__set__ call WebDriverWait before find_element - the tutorial's BasePageElement shows exactly that. What replaces the classic Java structure is Python's descriptor protocol plus the driver's explicit waits, with pytest or unittest fixtures owning browser setup and teardown. Keep the driver private, let page methods return the next page object, and let the test hold the assertions.
pitfalls: Descriptor access hides a wait on every read and write: the tutorial's BasePageElement waits up to 100 seconds, so a mistyped locator stalls the suite instead of failing fast - use short, explicit waits.
The driver must be closed in tearDown or a yield-fixture; without it every test leaks a browser session.
Locators kept as class attributes are shared and mutable; per-test values (like search_text_element) must live on the page instance, not the class.

variants.name: Playwright Python: class over Page with Locator attributes (sync or async)
variants.idiom_name: class holding a Page with Locator attributes, methods to navigate and act
variants.implementation_notes: Playwright's Python POM guide shows a plain class: the constructor takes the Page the fixture created and stores locator attributes (self.search_term_input = page.locator('[aria-label="Enter your search term"]')), and the methods call fill/press/goto; locators are lazy and auto-wait, so no expected_conditions are needed. Both the sync API (common in pytest fixtures) and the async API work, but one page class must not be shared between the two flavours because Playwright objects are not thread-safe. Choose it when the suite is Playwright-based; the Selenium variant is the classic one.
pitfalls: Playwright's sync and async APIs cannot be mixed inside one page object; calling sync methods from a running event loop raises.
Locators re-resolve on each use, but element handles and expect_* matchers do not: storing handles in attributes reintroduces staleness.
The browser and page are created and closed by the fixture; a page object that closes them (or that outlives them) breaks the next test.
